correctness.rationale: Reconstructs the sixteen-vertex GP(8,3) adjacency and the secure-guard quantifier for each outside vertex. Both complete finite programs enumerate every subset up to cardinality seven and find none secure below seven, exactly 336 at seven, then test all one-for-one exchanges and breadth-first distances from all vertices of every component. The second uses an independently defined 8-by-8 incidence graph, explicitly checked isomorphic by an edge-preserving 16-point bijection. Actual GP and incidence output files agree on 1392 jumps, 528 slides, one 336-state jump component, one 288-state slide component and 24 isolated edges, and all reported eccentricities. These are finite exhaustive proofs for the exact model; no extension to an infinite family claimed.

originality.rationale: The 2013 secure-domination article supplies a general definition and algorithms but does not itself supply the 336-state exchange network; the inspected 2015 primary PDF studies stability against removal of host edges, not guard replacements at fixed host; the 2014 original reconfiguration PDF treats unsecure dominating sets of variable cardinality under add/delete, and so does not imply the secure fixed-cardinality exchange statements. Relevant exact-host and parameter searches in research records and published sources found no comparable 24 K2 plus 288-state decomposition. Accessible historical claim about secure domination of the Heawood graph has different host graph and does not imply the present claim. value.rationale: The Möbius–Kantor graph is a canonical symmetric cubic incidence graph; secure minimum guard placements model single-attack defense with minimum resources. Beyond calculating a cardinality, the theorem completely classifies the optimal solution-space connectivity, exhibiting 24 separate two-state slide components alongside a connected 336-state jumping graph. Its precise degree and eccentricity distributions quantify a sharp operational obstruction introduced by adjacency-constrained guard moves. This is a natural exact reconfiguration invariant, not an arbitrary slice or a rephrased known minimum-value result.
